section.title: Habakkuk's Prayer
section.sectionRationale: The book closes not with an argument but with a psalm. Having heard God's answer, Habakkuk turns his questions into worship: a prayer for mercy, a vision of God coming in awesome power to save His people, and a final confession of joy that holds even if every crop fails. It is the resolution of the whole dialogue, faith learning to sing in the dark.
section.thesis: Habakkuk answers God's word with worship: he prays for mercy in wrath, rehearses God's mighty acts of salvation, trembles at the coming judgment, and then rises to a settled joy in the LORD that does not depend on circumstances, though the fig tree does not bud.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the opening prayer, in wrath remember mercy; the vision of God marching out in glory to save His people and crush the wicked; the prophet's trembling as he waits; and the summit of the book, though the fig tree does not bud, yet I will rejoice in the God of my salvation.

verses.text: This is a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to {{shigionoth|Shigionoth}}:
O LORD, I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds. Revive them in these years; make them known in these years. In Your wrath, remember mercy!

units.label: God comes in glory to save
units.note: a vision of the divine warrior

verses.text: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. {{selah|Selah}} His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth.
His radiance was like the sunlight; rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden.
Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps.
He stood and measured the earth; He looked and startled the nations; the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed. His ways are everlasting.
I saw the tents of Cushan in distress; the curtains of Midian were trembling.
Were You angry at the rivers, O LORD? Was Your wrath against the streams? Did You rage against the sea when You rode on Your horses, on Your chariots of salvation?
You brandished Your bow; You called for many arrows. Selah You split the earth with rivers.
The mountains saw You and quaked; torrents of water swept by. The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high.
Sun and moon stood still in their places at the flash of Your flying arrows, at the brightness of Your shining spear.
You marched across the earth with fury; You threshed the nations in wrath.
You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your {{mashiach|anointed}}. You crushed the head of the house of the wicked and stripped him from head to toe. Selah
With his own spear You pierced his head, when his warriors stormed out to scatter us, gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak.
You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters.
I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound. Decay entered my bones; I trembled where I stood. Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us.

units.label: Joy though everything fails
units.note: yet I will rejoice in the LORD

verses.text: Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls,
yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my {{yeshuah|salvation}}!
GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights! For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments.

shigionoth.gloss: A musical or liturgical term, probably indicating the tune, mood, or setting for the prayer, likely a passionate or wandering song. Its presence, with Selah and the closing note to the choirmaster, shows that chapter 3 is a psalm meant to be sung in the worship of God's people.

selah.gloss: A musical or literary marker found often in the Psalms, probably signaling a pause, an interlude, or a lifting up. It appears three times in this chapter, at verses 3, 9, and 13, inviting the worshiper to stop and weigh what has just been said about God's mighty acts.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, the one set apart with oil for God's service, especially the king. Here God goes forth to save His anointed and His people. The word is the root of Messiah and points beyond every earthly king to Christ, the true Anointed One whom God saves and vindicates.

yeshuah.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. The climax of Habakkuk's joy is that he rejoices in the God of his yeshuah. The word runs through the chapter, God rides on chariots of salvation and goes forth for the salvation of His people, and it is the root behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves.

basic.context: The final chapter is a prayer set to music, a psalm. Habakkuk has heard God's answers, and now he responds in worship. He asks God to act again in his own day and to remember mercy even in judgment. Then he paints a majestic picture of God coming in blazing power, the way He did at the exodus and Sinai, to rescue His people and crush the wicked. The vision leaves the prophet shaking. But he ends on the highest note in the book: even if every crop fails and every animal is gone, he will still rejoice in God his Savior.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter shows what to do with God's answers: turn them into worship. The prayer draws on Israel's memory of God's past acts of salvation to build confidence for the future. The famous ending is not naive optimism; it is faith that has counted the cost of total loss and still chooses joy in God Himself. It teaches that our joy can rest on who God is rather than on what we have.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is marked as a psalm: it is set according to Shigionoth, it uses Selah three times, and it ends with a note to the choirmaster. God goes forth to save His mashiach, His anointed, a word that points to the Messiah. And the whole prayer rises to yeshuah, salvation, the root behind the name Jesus: Habakkuk rejoices in the God of his salvation.
basic.typology: God riding out on chariots of salvation, crushing the head of the house of the wicked, echoes the promise of Genesis 3:15 and points to Christ who crushes the serpent. God going forth to save His anointed points to the Father raising and vindicating His Anointed One, Jesus. And the joy that survives total loss anticipates the resurrection hope that nothing can take away.
basic.christ: God saving His anointed and crushing the head of the wicked foreshadows the death and resurrection of Christ, in whom the serpent's head is crushed. The God of my salvation, yeshuah, is fully revealed in Jesus, whose very name means the LORD saves. And the joy of verse 18, held in the face of ruin, is the joy Paul echoes when he says rejoice in the Lord always, a joy grounded in the risen Christ.
basic.god: We learn that God is holy, gloriously powerful, and terrifying to His enemies, yet He comes for the salvation of His people. He is both the God of wrath and the God who is entreated to remember mercy. He is the strength of the weak, turning trembling knees into a deer's sure feet on the heights.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 33:2 and Judges 5 recall God coming from the south in glory. Genesis 3:15 lies behind crushing the head of the wicked. Philippians 4:4 and Romans 8:37 echo joy and triumph in God regardless of circumstances.
basic.oneStory: The book that began in protest ends in praise. Habakkuk learns to rest not on his circumstances but on the God of his salvation, whose past rescues guarantee the future and point to the ultimate rescue in Christ. His closing song is the voice of faith in every age, singing in the dark because the LORD is its strength.

context.literary:
Habakkuk 3 is built like a Psalm, and the frame is part of the point. A heading opens it in verse 1, and a musical direction closes it in verse 19, as if the whole chapter were a piece handed to the temple singers, who worked with lyres, harps and cymbals, 1 Chronicles 25:1. The book that began with the prophet shouting at God, 1:2, ends with the prophet's words being given to a choir.

Inside the frame there are four movements, and the grammar changes with each one. Verse 2 is petition, addressed to God as 'You' and 'O LORD.' Verses 3 to 7 describe God's coming in the third person: 'God came,' 'His glory,' 'His radiance.' At verse 8 the prophet turns and speaks straight to Him, and the 'You' runs unbroken through verse 15: You brandished, You split, You marched, You crushed, You trampled. Then verses 16 to 19 pass to the first person: 'I heard,' 'I trembled,' 'I will exult.' The prophet moves from reporting, to addressing, to owning what he has seen.

A small inclusio holds the chapter together. In verse 2 he says, 'I have heard the report of You,' and in verse 16 he says, 'I heard and trembled within.' The hearing that began as awe ends as a shaking of the whole body. The vision itself is bracketed by water: God marches, and in verse 15 He tramples the sea.

The last movement is a single long sentence. Verses 17 and 18 stack six failures, fig tree, vine, olive, field, fold and stall, and the main clause is held back until the two words 'yet I.' The syntax makes the reader wait through every loss before arriving at the joy, which is exactly what the prophet has done.
context.historical:
The most likely setting is the last decades of the seventh century before Christ. Nineveh had fallen in 612, and the Babylonians, whom God calls 'Chaldeans' in 1:6, were marching west. Judah's good king Josiah was dead, and the kings who followed him were ruled by foreign powers and their own corruption. By the time Jerusalem was burned in 586, the 'day of distress' of verse 16 had come.

The places named in verses 3 and 7 are all in the south and east, Teman, Mount Paran, Cushan and Midian. Teman lay in Edom, and Paran is the wilderness between Sinai and Canaan. Midian was where Moses spent his years of exile. To an Israelite singer this was the road God took when He came out of Sinai to bring Israel home, the route sung of in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Judges 5:4. The prophet is not writing a travel report. He is reciting the oldest hymns of the nation to put his people back inside the story of the exodus.

The imagery would also have sounded familiar to Judah's neighbours. The cultures around Israel told of a storm god who rode the clouds with lightning and spear. Habakkuk gives all of that to the LORD alone. The thunder, the arrows and the flashing spear are His, and so is the plague that follows behind Him in verse 5, a word that was also the name of a god of pestilence in Canaan. Here pestilence is not a deity to be feared but an attendant in the LORD's train.

The closing list in verses 17 and 18 is an accurate portrait of what an invading army did. Vines and olive trees take years to grow, fields could be burned, and flocks were driven off. A siege could strip a country of its food in a single season.
context.canonical:
Habakkuk 3 gathers up the older songs of Israel. Its roads from Teman and Paran repeat Deuteronomy 33:2, and its shaking mountains and pouring clouds recall the Song of Deborah, Judges 5:4-5. The tramped sea of verse 15 answers the Song of the Sea, Exodus 15:8-10, and the converging parallels with Psalm 77:16-19 are close enough that many readers hear the two psalmists drawing on one tradition. The sun and moon standing still in verse 11 recall Joshua's long day, Joshua 10:12-13. The deer's feet of verse 19 are the same line that David sings in Psalm 18:33.

Those songs set up the later prophets. Isaiah sees the LORD coming from Edom in garments stained from the winepress, Isaiah 63:1-3, and begs Him to wake as in days of old and cut Rahab to pieces, Isaiah 51:9-10. Habakkuk is a link in that chain. His line about waiting for the vision, 2:3, is the verse Hebrews 10:37-38 quotes when it urges believers to hold on until 'He who is coming will come and will not delay.'

In the New Testament the divine warrior is the returning Christ, with eyes like blazing fire, a robe dipped in blood, and the winepress of the fury of God, Revelation 19:11-15. The convulsing sun, moon and mountains of verses 10 and 11 reappear when the sixth seal is opened, Revelation 6:12-14.

The closing confession is picked up in a quiet way too. Mary sings 'my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,' Luke 1:47, which sounds very much like 'I will rejoice in the God of my salvation.' Paul, writing from prison, says he has learned to be content in plenty and in need, Philippians 4:11-13. Both of them sing Habakkuk's last note.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Habakkuk's complaints in chapters 1 and 2 got an answer, but the answer was an announcement, not an explanation. God told him the Chaldeans were coming and that the arrogant would fall in time. The prophet did not receive a map, he received a promise. Chapter 3 shows what he does with it. He prays, and he prays in the form that Israel always used when it did not understand what God was doing: it sang what God had done before.

He wants the hearers of the psalm to see the sequence he walked through. First comes hearing, then fear, then a plain request, 'revive them,' for God's work in their own day. Then memory, a long recital of God's marching in the past. Then the honest cost: the body breaks down when the prophet pictures the invasion. Only then comes the joy, and it is a joy chosen with the loss in full view.

He is also teaching them how to ask. 'In Your wrath, remember mercy' is not a demand that God drop His judgment. It assumes that judgment is just, and appeals to the character God declared to Moses, Exodus 34:6-7. The request is that, when God acts, mercy would still be on His mind.

For Judah the practical result is waiting. Verse 16 says he will wait quietly for the day of distress, which means the prophet is not promising escape. He is promising that the LORD will be there in it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The long vision of verses 3 to 15 is description, in poetry, of how God has acted and will act. It records Him marching, shaking the earth and crushing the head of a wicked house. It is not an instruction for human armies, and it gives no one permission to treat God's wars as a model for his own. God is the warrior here, and the people simply watch and are saved.

The last three verses are Habakkuk's own personal confession, and they carry a different weight. They describe what he resolved to do, and they work as a pattern, not a rule. The text does not promise that every believer who rejoices will see the fig tree bud again, or that the hungry will be fed. Notice the grammar: 'though' is repeated, and nothing in the poem says the harvest returns. What is promised is God Himself, 'my strength.' The application, then, is that the believer may bring honest sorrow and honest praise into one sentence, and that joy can be anchored in who God is when the circumstances give no support. Reading verse 19 as a guarantee of success or an easy path 'upon the heights' turns the poem into a slogan it never was.

debates.question: Is the vision of verses 3 to 15 a memory of the exodus, or a picture of something still to come?

views.label: A recital of what God did in the past
views.case: The places, Teman, Paran, Cushan and Midian, and the images of a trampled sea, the standing sun and the shaken mountains all come from the exodus and conquest, and the verbs in most of the section are in the past. Habakkuk is rehearsing what Israel already knew, as Psalm 77:16-19 does, to build trust for a new crisis.

views.label: A vision of a coming intervention
views.case: The prophet asks God to revive His work 'in these years' and says he must wait for the day of distress. Hebrew poetry often uses past forms for what is certain to happen, so the section can describe a future act in the past tense, an act the prophet has seen in the vision. Some then read it as pointing to the final day.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Israel's hymns used the past as the pattern of the future. The old acts are the guarantee, and the prophet prays that the same God will do the same kind of thing again, in his own generation and at the end.

debates.bearing: The text itself supports holding both. The prophet asks God to do now what he has heard He did then, and the New Testament takes the same pattern forward, Revelation 19:11-15, which shows that the final act is of one piece with the first.

debates.question: Who is God's 'anointed' in verse 13?

views.label: The king in David's line
views.case: The singular word 'anointed' normally names the king or priest in the Old Testament, and the verse sets the anointed beside 'Your people,' as Psalm 28:8 does: the LORD is the strength of His people, and a stronghold of salvation for His anointed. On this reading God marches to save the Davidic house from the Chaldean threat.

views.label: The whole people of God
views.case: Poetry often stands the singular for the community, and the verse pairs the salvation of 'Your people' with the salvation of 'Your anointed' as two lines saying one thing. The nation as a whole is God's chosen, set apart by His choice.

views.label: The Messiah, ultimately
views.case: Whatever the prophet had in view, the Church has read the verse in the light of the King who is the head of His people. In Christ the king and the people are saved together, for He is raised and they are raised in Him.

debates.bearing: The first two readings fit the poem's own setting, and the third is where the line finally lands. A reader can hold that the immediate sense was the king or the nation without losing the New Testament's fulfilment in the one Anointed who carries His people with Him.

debates.question: What is the 'day of distress' that the prophet waits for in verse 16?

views.label: The downfall of the invaders
views.case: The BSB renders the line as a day of distress coming 'upon the people who invade us.' The prophet then waits quietly for God to bring down the Chaldeans, as chapter 2 has already promised.

views.label: The invasion itself
views.case: The Hebrew of the clause is hard, and some translators take it as a wait for the day when the invader arrives against Judah. Then the prophet is accepting that the crisis will come on his own people first, and the joy of verse 18 has to survive that.

debates.bearing: Either way, the prophet does not escape the day, he waits through it. The two readings can be heard together, since Judah's distress comes first, and then the oppressor's. Both belong to the single hope of verse 18.

study.originalLanguages:
Habakkuk begins his prayer with two verbs that frame the chapter. 'I have heard the report of You' uses shama', hear, and when he says 'I stand in awe' the verb is yare', the ordinary Hebrew word for fear. Translators soften it, but the prophet is saying that what he has heard frightens him. The two verbs return in verse 16, 'I heard and trembled.'

'Revive them' in verse 2 is a command to God, from the verb chayah, live, in an intensive stem, 'make alive again.' The same verb is in Psalm 85:6, 'Will You not revive us again?' The phrase 'in these years' is literally 'in the midst of years,' so the prophet asks God to act within history, between what He did and what He will do.

The last clause of verse 2 sets two words side by side. 'Wrath' is rogez, from a root that means trembling or agitation, and the root comes back in verse 16 when the prophet's own body 'trembled.' God's agitation of the earth becomes the prophet's agitation. 'Mercy' is racham, tied to the word for the womb, so that it names the feeling a mother has for the child she bore. He asks that when God is shaking everything, the womb-like tenderness would be remembered.

In verse 4 the rays flashing from God's hand are literally 'horns,' qarnayim, since a horn was the natural picture of a beam of light. The verb built on the same root describes Moses' face when he came down from Sinai, Exodus 34:29, so the phrase quietly puts the glory of Sinai on God's own hand.

In verse 8 the war chariots are called 'chariots of salvation,' so that God's very machinery of war is named for rescue. The root yasha' sounds three times in the chapter, in verse 8, verse 13, where the people and the anointed are both saved, and in verse 18, where it becomes 'my salvation.'

In verse 13 'crushed' translates a verb for shattering, machats, the verb of Psalm 68:21, 'God will crush the heads of His enemies.' It is not the verb of Genesis 3:15, which is shuph, so the link to the serpent is one of image, a head struck down, and not of vocabulary.

In verse 19 'strength' is chayil, a word used of an army as well as of vigour. The commander of the heavenly armies has become the prophet's own force, and he calls Him 'GOD the Lord.' The last picture is the deer's feet, and the word for the 'heights' is the one used of high places that Israel was to tread on in Deuteronomy 33:29.

typology.type: The divine warrior who comes to rescue, Habakkuk 3:3-13
typology.fulfillment: God marching out in fire and storm to save His people is the pattern, and Revelation completes it. The rider on the white horse is named Faithful and True, His eyes are like blazing fire, and He treads the winepress of the wrath of God, Revelation 19:11-15, which recalls Isaiah 63:1-3. The correspondence is that salvation arrives with real judgment. The escalation is that He is a person, with the name The Word of God, and His weapon is a sword from His mouth. The type is not a fixed battle plan: the cross comes first, and the Warrior who wins is the Lamb, Revelation 5:5-6.

In the Old Testament the sea stands for the waters of chaos that only God can master, Psalm 89:9-10 and Isaiah 51:9-10. Habakkuk sees God ride over them. In the Gospels the pattern is met in a person: Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, Mark 4:39, and the disciples ask who this is that the sea obeys Him, Mark 4:41. He walks on the sea, Matthew 14:25. The type falls short in that the exodus waters opened for Israel, while Jesus does not part the sea but stands above it. At the end the sea is no more, Revelation 21:1.

typology.type: Creation shaken at the coming of God, Habakkuk 3:6, 10-11
typology.fulfillment: The mountains that quake and the sun and moon that stand still at God's brightness find their New Testament counterpart at the cross. Darkness came over all the land, Matthew 27:45, and at His death the earth quaked and the rocks were split, Matthew 27:51. The correspondence is that creation reacts when God acts. The escalation is that the Judge is the One who is judged: the convulsion is the sign of the Day of the LORD falling on the Son. Revelation 6:12-14 shows the same signs at the final day.

typology.type: Joy through the loss of everything, Habakkuk 3:17-18
typology.fulfillment: Habakkuk's decision to rejoice with empty stalls is lived out most completely by Christ, 'who for the joy set before Him endured the cross,' Hebrews 12:2. He gave up every comfort and kept His hold on the Father. The early Christians followed Him and 'joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property,' Hebrews 10:34, because they had a better possession. The type falls short only in that Habakkuk's joy looks forward to a deliverance he could not name, while the believer's looks back to a resurrection that has already happened.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most clearly by pattern. A holy God comes in radiance to save His people, and the Gospels show the coming. When Jesus is transfigured, 'His face shone like the sun,' Matthew 17:2, and Moses and Elijah, standing in glory, talk with Him about His 'departure,' which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:29-31. The word behind 'departure' is exodos, so the conversation is about the new exodus that Habakkuk's hymn looks back to. The old song of God coming from Teman now has a name and an address.

The detail in verse 4 that God's power is 'hidden' in His hand is worth pausing over. The radiance is real, but the power is veiled. Paul says the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6, and that Christ is the power of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. That power was never more hidden than in the cross, where He 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them, Colossians 2:15. The warrior who crushes the enemy's head wins the way Habakkuk 2:4 said the righteous live: by faith, with the outcome unseen.

It leads to Christ by the 'anointed.' God goes out 'for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed,' verse 13. Hebrews says that in the days of His flesh Jesus offered prayers 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard,' Hebrews 5:7. The Anointed One really was saved, by resurrection, Acts 2:24, and the verse puts people and anointed together because the Anointed does not rise alone. His people are raised with Him and seated with Him, Ephesians 2:6.

It leads to Christ by name. The root of 'salvation' in verses 13 and 18 is the root of the name Jesus, which the angel said means He 'will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. Mary's song, 'my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,' Luke 1:47, is Habakkuk's last line carried into the first chapter of the Gospel.

Finally, Christ is the answer to the prayer in verse 2. 'In Your wrath, remember mercy' is answered at the cross, where mercy and wrath meet in the same act, Romans 3:25-26.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Habakkuk's 'head of the house of the wicked' was a historical enemy, and the verse does not mention Satan. The link to Genesis 3:15 is one of image, not of vocabulary. The New Testament gives the right to read the pattern forward, in Colossians 2:15 and Hebrews 2:14, so that is where the claim should rest, not in the chapter alone.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter says of God is that He is both near and holy. He is 'the Holy One,' verse 3, the title the prophet used in 1:12 when he asked how such a God could use the Chaldeans. The question that troubled chapter 1 has not been answered by argument. It has been answered by a view of God who is bigger than the question.

He is sovereign over every part of creation. Rivers, sea, sun, moon and mountains all respond to Him, and the poem's question in verse 8, 'Were You angry at the rivers?', is an answer in disguise. His anger is not at water. The ancient world pictured the sea as a power that could threaten the gods, and the Old Testament uses the picture to say that the LORD has already beaten it, Psalm 74:13-14. What He opposes is the wicked house of verse 13, and what He is doing is saving.

He is just and merciful, and the prophet prays as one who knows both. The appeal of verse 2 rests on the self-description in Exodus 34:6-7, where the LORD is 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger,' and yet 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.' Habakkuk does not choose between these. He asks that, in the moment of wrath, mercy would be remembered, and the New Testament shows how both are satisfied in one place.

He is patient and He takes His time. The vision 'awaits an appointed time,' 2:3, and God does not explain the delay. Yet He is not absent while it lasts. He gives His people strength, the strength of an army, and sets their feet on the heights.

He is the God who can be trusted when the evidence goes the other way. The prophet's final cry rests not on a favourable forecast but on the character of the One he has seen, and on the memory of what that One has done.

For worship, the chapter teaches that there is a place for fear and a place for joy and that they belong in the same song. It shows that lament may turn into praise, not by being skipped, but by being carried through to the end. It also teaches us to remember: the hymns of the past are not museum pieces but tools for the day when nothing makes sense. Sing the old songs in the new crisis, and let the God of Sinai be your God in the siege.

crossReferences.note: Moses' blessing opens with the LORD coming from Sinai, Seir and Paran with myriads of holy ones and fire at His right hand. Habakkuk picks up the same southern route and the same fire. He treats the old blessing as a living pattern: the God who came to bring Israel into a land can come again to deal with the nation that has taken it.

Deborah's victory song has the LORD march from Seir and Edom while the earth trembles and the mountains quake. Habakkuk shares the setting and the effect on creation, but changes the audience: the song of a battle won becomes the prayer of a people about to lose one, who trust that He who won it before can win it again.

The psalmist, in his own distress, remembers how the waters saw God and were shaken, with clouds, arrows and lightning. His 'way through the mighty waters' with footprints no one could find is like Habakkuk's trampled sea. Both poets move from anguish to memory, and from memory to trust.

The sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance on its enemies. Habakkuk 3:11 uses the picture in a wider sense: sun and moon halt before the flash of God's arrows. The old miracle becomes a sign that the heavenly lights are His servants, and obey Him in war.

David says, 'He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights,' in the same psalm that has God riding on the storm. Habakkuk closes with nearly the same line. He has borrowed a victor's thanksgiving and put it in the mouth of a man who has not yet seen any victory, and it becomes an act of faith.

Among the covenant curses are vineyards that give no wine and olive trees whose fruit drops off. When Habakkuk lists the vine and the olive among the losses of verse 17, he is naming the curse of the covenant, falling on Judah. His joy is therefore not blind to the reason for the loss, and it is chosen all the same.

Joel's locust plague leaves the field ruined, the new wine dry, the oil failing and the fig tree withered, and he ends the list with 'the joy of mankind has dried up.' Habakkuk's list is similar and his answer is the opposite: where joy dried up, he vows to rejoice in the LORD, not in the produce.

The vision 'awaits an appointed time' and will 'not delay,' and the righteous live by faith. Chapter 3 is the lived form of that sentence. The prophet waits, verse 16, and then lives by faith, verses 17 to 19. Hebrews 10:37-38 quotes this very passage to urge believers to endure until the coming One comes.

A figure comes from Edom with stained garments, 'mighty to save,' having trodden the winepress alone. The southern direction and the combination of salvation with judgment match Habakkuk 3. The two prophets describe one Warrior, and Revelation 19:11-15 later shows that He is the returning Christ.

'Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song.' The line quotes the Song of the Sea, and its words, salvation and strength, are the very words that close Habakkuk's prayer. The prophet is singing the exodus song in the dark.

Paul writes from prison that he has learned to be content in having plenty and in having need, and that he can do all things through Christ who gives him strength. The pattern is the same as Habakkuk's: contentment is not a mood but a learned trust, and strength is given by Another.

Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and was heard. In the light of Habakkuk 3:13, God going out to save His anointed is fulfilled in the Father's raising of the Son, and the prophet's faith in the face of distress finds its perfect form.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God ruling the waters and the lights of the sky, Genesis 1:2 and 1:14-18. Habakkuk's vision is that rule in action: the sea is trampled and the sun and moon stand still. What is new in the chapter is the enemy. After Genesis 3 the world contains a wicked house that devours the weak, 1:13 and 3:14, and the vision is the answer to Habakkuk's first question, 'How long?' The God who made the earth has not stopped caring what is done on it.

The chapter also sits at a hinge in Israel's history. Behind it are the exodus, Sinai and the conquest, which are the proofs that God saves. Ahead of it is the exile, in which the temple is burned and the land is stripped, and the people have to sing without the signs. Habakkuk teaches them how. The hymns of the past go with them into the foreign land, and the Psalms that follow in exile lean on the same memory.

The New Testament carries that line to its centre. At the cross the darkness and the shaking happen, Matthew 27:45 and 27:51, and the Anointed is saved by resurrection. The risen Christ now sits at the right hand of the Father, and His people share His joy while the world still groans, Romans 8:18-23. They are the 'I' of verse 18, rejoicing before the harvest, and they are asked to wait.

The new creation answers the six losses of verse 17. Micah says that each person will sit under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to frighten him, Micah 4:4. In Revelation the tree of life gives fruit every month and there is no more curse, Revelation 22:2-3. The sea that threatened is no more, Revelation 21:1, and the radiance of verse 4 is replaced by something better: the city needs no sun, for the glory of God lights it and the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The prophet's joy in the dark becomes a joy in the full light.

sermon.title: I Will Rejoice!
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Habakkuk, this message expounds Habakkuk 3:1-19, the prophet's closing prayer and his triumphant joy in the God of his salvation even if the fig tree does not bud. A faithful, orthodox handling of this exact movement.

quiz.q: What kind of writing is Habakkuk 3?

options.text: A prayer set to music, a psalm, marked by Shigionoth, Selah, and a note to the choirmaster.
options.note: The chapter is a sung prayer, turning God's answers into worship.

options.text: A prayer of praise responding in worship to God's answer.
options.note: True to its content, though it misses that it is specifically a psalm set for music.

options.text: A list of rules for temple sacrifices.
options.note: It is worship, but a sung prayer, not a manual of sacrificial law.

options.text: A legal contract between Habakkuk and Babylon.
options.note: It is a psalm of prayer and praise, not a contract.

quiz.q: What does Habakkuk ask for in verse 2?

options.text: That God would revive His work in these years and, in His wrath, remember mercy.
options.note: He prays for God to act again and to temper judgment with mercy.

options.text: That God would show mercy even in the midst of the coming judgment.
options.note: This is half his prayer; he also asks God to revive His mighty work in their day.

options.text: That the Babylonians would be spared all judgment.
options.note: He asks mercy for God's people; the oppressor remains under judgment.

options.text: That God would destroy Judah completely and without mercy.
options.note: He pleads for mercy in the midst of wrath, not for total destruction.

quiz.q: What does the vision in verses 3 to 15 portray?

options.text: God coming in awesome glory as a warrior to save His people and crush the wicked.
options.note: The theophany recalls the exodus and Sinai, God marching out for salvation.

options.text: God's overwhelming power over creation and the nations.
options.note: True, but it leaves out the purpose: He marches out to save His people.

options.text: A description of Habakkuk's travels.
options.note: The place names evoke God's past acts of salvation, not the prophet's journeys.

options.text: The Babylonians triumphing over God.
options.note: God crushes the head of the house of the wicked; He is not defeated.

quiz.q: What is the summit of the book in verses 17 to 18?

options.text: Though every crop and flock fails, yet Habakkuk will rejoice in the God of his salvation.
options.note: Joy grounded in God Himself, not in circumstances, is the book's climax.

options.text: Choosing to find joy in God even in the face of total loss.
options.note: A faithful paraphrase, though the striking picture of the failed fig tree and empty stalls is the point.

options.text: A demand that God explain everything first.
options.note: He moves past demanding answers to resting in God's character.

options.text: A promise that the harvest will always be abundant.
options.note: He rejoices precisely when the harvest fails, resting in God alone.

quiz.q: How does the salvation of God's anointed in 3:13 point to Christ?

options.text: The word anointed, mashiach, points beyond every king to the Messiah, and crushing the head of the wicked echoes the promise of Genesis 3:15.
options.note: God saving His anointed and crushing the wicked finds its fullness in Christ's victory.

options.text: It celebrates God going forth to save and vindicate His anointed one.
options.note: True, and the word mashiach and the head-crushing draw the line specifically to Christ.

options.text: It teaches that the Messiah would be a Babylonian king.
options.note: The anointed is God's own, saved and vindicated, fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ whatsoever.
options.note: Mashiach is the root of Messiah, and the head-crushing echoes Genesis 3:15.

questions: Habakkuk turned God's answers into worship rather than just information. How might you make praise, not only understanding, your response to what God has shown you?
The prophet built his confidence by remembering God's past acts of salvation. What specific rescues in your own life, or in the gospel, can you rehearse to steady your faith today?
In wrath, remember mercy was his prayer. Where do you need to ask God for mercy in the middle of a hard season, for yourself or for others?
Habakkuk chose joy in God even imagining total loss, no figs, no crops, no flocks. What would it look like for your joy to rest on God Himself rather than on your circumstances?
God made the trembling prophet's feet like a deer's on the heights. Where do you feel unsteady right now, and how might God's strength carry you through it?

translationNotes.note: Shigionoth is probably a musical term indicating the tune or mood for the prayer; it marks chapter 3 as a psalm for worship.
Selah, also at verses 9 and 13, is probably a musical or literary term signaling a pause or interlude for reflection.
Anointed translates mashiach, the root of Messiah; it can denote the king or the covenant people, and points ultimately to Christ.
The closing line, for the choirmaster with stringed instruments, is a liturgical direction confirming the chapter was sung in Israel's worship.
